chapter: Hal, Tony Giardino and other musicians
title: How the New Orleans dance work season ran
summary: Saturday-night dances, picnics, Lent, and few clubs in those days.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Well, talking about Dave Perkins, you see, I used to make quite a few jobs, you know, in and around town, out of town too. And sometimes I couldn't make the job with him, see, and he'd say to me, come and say to me, see, man, he said, you know, you're playing with, all you're doing is playing with them Sweet Marie bands, he used to call them, band with them fiddles in it, see. Sweet Marie bands. Sweet Marie bands, see. And I used to tell him, I said, well, Dave, I said, man, I said, those are the fellas that are working, see. A lot of the fiddle players, you know what I mean, in them days, like Charlie and Max Fink and Rainey Solomon and Joe Calro, all them guys were playing, you know, all fiddle men, you know what I mean? And they got jobs, and they got study jobs most of them too, you know what I mean? The other guys were playing these once in a while jobs, you know? And I had to make money, I couldn't just play them once. And it was, you know, New Orleans was really a big, like a big Saturday night deal, you know what I mean? The fellas played on Saturday nights, and then during the summertime they played picnics out of different places. But it wasn't like it is now, and during the Lent time the only time the bands played most of them was on St. Joseph's night. People really didn't go to dances, you know, but now they go any time, any time to dances. But, and then, like I said, of course, there wasn't too many clubs around in them days too, you know, there wasn't too many clubs.
